title: Plasma concentration after a single oral dose

segs.text: Module five, objective two. The plasma concentration after a single oral dose. C p is the plasma concentration of drug at a time t after the dose, in milligrams per liter. One equation gives it at any time from five inputs: F, the fraction of the dose absorbed; the dose, D zero; V D, the volume of distribution; k a, the absorption rate constant; and k, the elimination rate constant. It applies to a single oral dose in one compartment, with first order absorption and first order elimination.

card.m: C<sub>p</sub>: plasma concentration at time t, mg/L
F: fraction absorbed   D<sub>0</sub>: dose, mg   V<sub>D</sub>: L
one dose, one compartment, first order in and out

segs.text: The equation is built as drug in minus drug out. Inside its bracket are two exponentials that start equal, so at time zero the bracket is zero and the oral curve starts at zero concentration. k a is the larger constant, so the absorption term shrinks fast and the elimination term, with k, shrinks slowly. Early on the difference between them grows, which is the rise; once the absorption term is nearly gone, the curve follows the elimination term alone, which is the slow fall.

card.m: bracket: e<sup>−kt</sup> − e<sup>−k<sub>a</sub>t</sup> = drug in minus drug out
t = 0: e<sup>0</sup> − e<sup>0</sup> = 0, so C<sub>p</sub> starts at 0
e<sup>−k<sub>a</sub>t</sup>: falls fast   e<sup>−kt</sup>: falls slowly
rise, then the fall follows k alone

segs.text: The fraction in front combines F, the dose, k a, V D and the difference of the rate constants into one number. It is not C zero, the starting concentration of an I V bolus, because the bracket is always less than one, so no point on the oral curve reaches it. She said, this big portion right here does not represent C zero. F and the dose sit on the top, so doubling the dose doubles C p at every time, and V D sits on the bottom, so a larger volume gives a lower curve. The textbook adds that the timing of the curve, when it rises and falls, is set by k a and k alone.

card.m: not C<sub>0</sub>: the bracket is always < 1
D<sub>0</sub> × 2 → every C<sub>p</sub> × 2; e.g. her Example 1, 500 → 1000 mg: front number 25.76 → 51.52 mg/L

segs.text: The equation reads: C p equals F times k a times D zero, over V D times k a minus k, all times e to the minus k t minus e to the minus k a t. C p comes out in milligrams per liter with the dose in milligrams, V D in liters, both rate constants per hour and t in hours since the dose, and the line is on the equation sheet, page one.

card.m: C<sub>p</sub> mg/L, D<sub>0</sub> mg, V<sub>D</sub> L, k<sub>a</sub> and k hr<sup>−1</sup>, t hr; on the sheet, p. 1

segs.text: In her problems the equation often arrives with the fraction already worked out as one leading number, P, in milligrams per liter, and a question asks for a parameter inside it. Her slide Example two gives C p equals seventy five e to the minus zero point two two t, minus seventy five e to the minus two point seven five t. She expects the larger exponent to be read as k a, and the textbook explains why: most oral drugs have shorter absorption half-lives than elimination half-lives. To find V D, P is set equal to the fraction and the line is rearranged: V D equals F times k a times D zero, over P times k a minus k.

card.m: larger exponent = k<sub>a</sub> = 2.75 hr<sup>−1</sup>; smaller = k = 0.22 hr<sup>−1</sup>

segs.text: Her in class practice two: a seven hundred fifty milligram oral dose, eighty four percent bioavailable, gives C p equals twenty three point two times the bracket of e to the minus zero point one eight two t and e to the minus zero point eight seven two t, and V D and the half-life of elimination are asked. The exponents give k a, zero point eight seven two per hour, and k, zero point one eight two per hour. V D is asked with P, F and the dose given, so the rearranged line answers it, and V D is thirty four point three liters. So each milligram per liter in the plasma corresponds to about thirty four milligrams of drug in the body.

card.m: C<sub>p</sub> = 23.2(e<sup>−0.182t</sup> − e<sup>−0.872t</sup>) mg/L, D<sub>0</sub> = 750 mg, F = 0.84

segs.text: The second answer is the half-life, and with no qualifier that means the elimination half-life, so it uses k, the smaller exponent. She said, If it's just T one half, then your assumption is that I'm looking for the half-life of elimination. The half-life equals zero point six nine three over k, a line she says is never on the equation sheet, and here it is three point eight hours.

card.m: no qualifier: elimination half-life, use k

segs.text: In her slide Example two, five hundred milligrams at eighty seven percent bioavailability gives a V D of six point three liters. Quiz three gave thirty times the bracket of e to the minus zero point one three three t and e to the minus zero point nine three four t, a five hundred milligram dose and eighty two percent bioavailability, and keyed fifteen point nine liters. Dividing the dose by thirty, as if thirty were C zero, gives sixteen point seven, close enough to look right, and that is the trap. The other traps are leaving out V D and losing the k a minus k term when rearranging.
